attempts.label: DANDI:000166
attempts.entry_title: Layer-specific features of mouse V1 units (Senzai et al. 2019)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Senzai, Fernandez-Ruiz and Buzsaki (2019) on dandiset 000166, which holds one session from each of 19 mice recorded with a 64-site linear probe in V1, with spike-sorted units, LFP, the raw signal, brain state and UP/DOWN intervals and laser pulse times. It tests the unit counts and waveform classes, the CCG-based detection of monosynaptic connections, the optogenetic tagging, the gamma ICA and coherence clusters, the laminar LFP power, cross-frequency coupling and 3-6 Hz phase locking, the K-means unit clusters and the layer features of firing and connections that rest on them, and the DOWN state-active neurons. Depth is aligned on the MUA power peak, as the CSD landmarks cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Senzai et al. (2019) from dandiset 000166

outcomes.statement: The layer 3/4 border sink of the DOWN-UP transition of non-REM slow oscillations (landmark b) lies slightly but significantly deeper than the early light-evoked sink (b') in the same mice, by 39 ± 49 um.
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 1F
outcomes.quote: Sink b, associated with the “UP” state of slow oscillation during non-REM sleep, was slightly but significantly deeper than the light-evoked sink b′ in the layer 3/4 border (39 ± 49 μm
outcomes.notes: The light-evoked CSD needs the times of the 520 nm flashes in the 13 stimulated mice. The dataset holds them in 2 files only, the `Visual laser` tables of YMV05 and YMV08 (498 intervals of 0.4 s each, plus the optogenetic pulses). With 2 mice a signed-rank test cannot reach p < 0.05 (its smallest two-sided p is 0.5). The DOWN-UP half of the comparison is computed under fig1g-landmark-distances-consistent.

outcomes.statement: The other CSD sinks and sources of slow oscillations (a, d, e) occur at the same depths as the corresponding light-evoked sinks and sources (a', d', e').
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 1F
outcomes.quote: whereas the other sinks and sources occurred at the same depth as those seen with visual stimulation (p > 0.05, signed rank test)
outcomes.notes: Needs the light-evoked landmarks a', d' and e', which need the flash times of 13 mice; the dataset has them for 2 (see fig1f-sink-b-deeper). It also depends on fig1f-sink-b-deeper.

outcomes.statement: The distances between the five depth landmarks (the MUA power peak c and the CSD landmarks a, b, d, e) vary by less than 100 um from mouse to mouse.
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 2; Figure 1G
outcomes.quote: Importantly, the distances between the five landmarks were consistent across animals and varied <100 μm from mouse to mouse ( Figure 1 G; n = 19)
outcomes.notes: Every reading was run (CSD as the unsmoothed second difference of the claims file and, as a variant, over two sites; windows 0-100 and 0-50 ms; "varied" as the range and as the largest deviation from the mean). The data columns are in depth order (for each file, the best-correlated site in the 100-500 Hz LFP is an adjacent one for 50 to 63 of the 64 sites, median 58). The MUA peak c is found in all 19 mice, but the rule (most negative CSD for b above c and d below it, most positive for a above b and e below d, each over the whole half of the probe) places all five landmarks in only 15 or 16 mice, and among those the ranges of the adjacent distances are 220 to 620 um (largest deviations 114 to 420 um), against less than 110 um. The CSD maps of all mice show that the rule picks probe-edge values in some mice (a or b within 3 sites of the top in YMV09 and YMV13, d or e within 3 sites of the bottom in YMV09) and places a one site above b in 7 mice. The paper places the landmarks by eye ("the most prominent current source density (CSD) sinks and sources", Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns, paragraph 1; asterisks in Figure 1D), and neither it nor the claims file gives a rule that can be run, so the claim is blocked with every reading shown. The question for the paper's authors is in the findings. The other laminar claims are tested with depth relative to c, which needs no other landmark.
deviations: DOWN-UP transitions are the dataset's UP onsets that follow a DOWN interval, averaged over the 1000 s of each session holding the most of them (114 to 1,541 transitions), not over the whole session.
MUA power (landmark c) is computed from the two 30 s raw blocks used for the waveforms, not the whole session.
Site 0 is taken as the most superficial, as the files' rel_y runs from -1 to -64; the electrode table gives no depth.

outcomes.statement: Clustering the 64 sites by their pairwise gamma (30-100 Hz) coherence with a gradient-descent algorithm gives six clusters whose five boundaries are consistent across mice in normalized depth.
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figures 2A, 2B
outcomes.quote: the recording sites were clustered on the basis of their resulting cross-coherence matrix, resulting in six clusters whose five boundaries were consistent across animals when projected into normalized depth coordinates

statistics.test: signed rank test for cluster boundaries across animals

outcomes.notes: Under the readings the criterion lists with six clusters imposed (reading b) and each mouse's boundaries compared with the across-mouse median, the claim holds: a six-cluster solution is found in all 18 mice (contiguous in depth in 14) and no boundary differs from the median (signed-rank p 0.74 to 1). The other readings fail: left free, the clustering converges to 8 to 20 clusters from 64 random labels (6 to 10 from 16), and against the matching IC boundaries three of five boundaries differ (p = 0.033, 0.013, 0.028; median differences 3.5 to 5.8 sites). The comparison with the across-mouse median can hardly fail by construction, so the outcome shows only that six clusters can be placed with boundaries spread around common depths (medians 21, 13.5 and 3 sites above c and 4.5 and 12.5 below it). Each boundary ranges across mice by 31 to 40 sites (620 to 800 um; boundary 1 from 46.5 to 12.5 sites above c), wider than the 220 to 620 um spread of the landmark distances that fig1g-landmark-distances-consistent calls inconsistent. The criterion's reading (b) for the cluster number together with its reading (b) for the boundaries can hardly fail; this is asked of a reader in questions/000166.yaml.
deviations: Coherence is the magnitude-squared coherence in 1 s Hann segments, averaged over 30-100 Hz, on the waking blocks of the ICA (up to 600 s per mouse).

The energy-gap moves follow the STAR Methods (Gamma coherence and gradient descent clustering). The number of random initial clusters is not given; 64 (and 16, shown) are used for reading (a), and 6 (or 8 when no run of 20 ends with six) for reading (b); the lowest-energy run of 20 is kept.
Boundary k is the number of sites in clusters 1 to k minus 0.5, exact for contiguous clusters.

Depth is taken in sites relative to landmark c (the MUA power peak), in place of the paper's normalized depth, which warps depth between all five landmarks (STAR Methods, Depth normalization) and so needs a, b, d and e, which no rule given in the paper places (fig1g-landmark-distances-consistent). Aligning on c is an assumption.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: The depth distribution of the six gamma coherence clusters corresponds roughly to the six cortical layers in each brain state and does not differ between states.
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figure 2B; Figure S2E
outcomes.quote: The depth distribution of the six gamma coherence clusters corresponded roughly to the six cortical layers in each brain state ( Figures 2 B and S2 ; p > 0.05, ANOVA for comparison across different states)

statistics.test: ANOVA for comparison across different states

outcomes.notes: No boundary of the six-cluster solutions differs across waking, non-REM and REM (one-way ANOVA p 0.53, 0.58, 0.71, 0.86, 0.87; Kruskal-Wallis p 0.41 to 0.87; 18 mice per state); the boundary means differ by at most 3.2 sites between states (boundary 1, 23.4 against 20.2 sites above c).
deviations: Non-REM and REM coherence come from up to 600 s and 300 s of each state; six clusters imposed as in fig2b reading (b).

Depth is taken in sites relative to landmark c (the MUA power peak), in place of the paper's normalized depth, which warps depth between all five landmarks (STAR Methods, Depth normalization) and so needs a, b, d and e, which no rule given in the paper places (fig1g-landmark-distances-consistent). Aligning on c is an assumption.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: ICA of the 30-100 Hz LFP yields six main independent components whose spatial loadings are highly consistent across mice and whose depth distribution is related to the anatomical layers.
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: ICA yielded six main independent components (ICs) that were highly consistent across animals (p < 0.001, Spearman’s correlation for ICs spatial loadings)

statistics.test: Spearman's correlation for ICs spatial loadings

outcomes.notes: With the six highest-variance ICs (reading a), each mouse's loading correlates positively with the mean of the other mice for all six ICs (median Spearman rho 0.87, 0.84, 0.75, 0.58, 0.58, 0.94 from the surface), with signed-rank p below 0.001 for five (p 7.6e-6 to 0.00033) and p = 0.0019 for IC 4, so the criterion's p < 0.001 for each of the six fails for one. The pairwise reading gives p below 0.001 for five ICs and 0.02 for IC 4. With the six confined ICs (reading b), ICs 1-3 pass and ICs 4-6 do not (p 0.0056 to 0.016). The ICs lie in depth from a median 26 sites above c to 24 below it. In 17 of 18 mice one of the six peaks at or near the deepest site and carries 0.03 to 0.71 of the band variance. This deepest IC is main IC 6 under reading (a) and is spread over depth in 9 of 18 mice, so there it is also counted as volume conducted in ica-volume-conduction-fraction reading (a); its loading is the most consistent IC across mice (median rho 0.94). Reading (b) leaves the spread ICs out and fails for ICs 4-6. 18 mice (YMV19 has no state table).
deviations: The gamma ICA (STAR Methods, Independent Component Analysis of LFPs) is fitted on up to 600 s of waking per mouse (the longest `Awake` epochs of at least 30 s), with scikit-learn's FastICA on the first ten PCs of the 30-100 Hz LFP in place of runica (EEGLAB infomax, not available in Python); the whole-session reading of fig2c is not run.

Depth is taken in sites relative to landmark c (the MUA power peak), in place of the paper's normalized depth, which warps depth between all five landmarks (STAR Methods, Depth normalization) and so needs a, b, d and e, which no rule given in the paper places (fig1g-landmark-distances-consistent). Aligning on c is an assumption.

Each mouse's loading is compared with the mean of the other mice (leave-one-out), over aligned sites held by at least 5 other mice, and the p is a signed-rank test of the 18 correlations against zero; the claims file names the comparison but not the test of the correlations.
A loading is confined when fewer than half the sites exceed half its peak absolute value (a choice, stated; used for reading b).
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: ICA removes volume-conducted currents, which account for 0.34 ± 0.11 of the V1 gamma LFP variance.
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: This method has the additional advantage of removing volume-conducted currents ( Fernández-Ruiz et al., 2012 ) that accounted for 0.34 ± 0.11 of V1 gamma LFP variance
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), the ICs whose loadings are spread over depth (half the sites or more above half their peak) carry 0.534 ± 0.163 of the gamma variance (1 to 4 such ICs per mouse); reading (b), one minus the share of the six main ICs, is 0.056 ± 0.022. Neither is within 0.34 ± 0.11. The ten PCs hold 0.99 of the band-passed variance, so reading (b) is bound to be small. In 9 of 18 mice the main IC 6 of fig2c reading (a) is one of the spread ICs, so reading (a) here and fig2c reading (a) count the same component in two roles; under the consistent pairing (spread ICs as volume conducted, confined ICs as main), fig2c reading (b) fails for ICs 4-6 and fig2d still fails.
deviations: The gamma ICA (STAR Methods, Independent Component Analysis of LFPs) is fitted on up to 600 s of waking per mouse (the longest `Awake` epochs of at least 30 s), with scikit-learn's FastICA on the first ten PCs of the 30-100 Hz LFP in place of runica (EEGLAB infomax, not available in Python); the whole-session reading of fig2c is not run.
The spread rule (half the sites or more above half the peak loading) is a choice; the claims file reads spread as uniform over depth (Fernandez-Ruiz et al. 2012) without a threshold.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: The three superficial gamma ICs have larger relative power than the three deep ones (0.14 ± 0.04 against 0.08 ± 0.03).
outcomes.source: Results, Anchoring Mesoscopic Patterns to Physiological Landmarks, paragraph 3; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: The superficial gamma ICs had a significantly larger power compared with the deeper ones (top three versus bottom three; Figures 2 D and S4 ; 0.14 ± 0.04 versus 0.08 ± 0.03 relative power for ICs 1–3 versus 4–6
outcomes.notes: Relative power of ICs 1-3 is 0.106 ± 0.101 (within 0.14 ± 0.04) and of ICs 4-6 0.209 ± 0.200 (outside 0.08 ± 0.03), 54 values each; the deep ICs are larger (rank-sum p = 0.035), the opposite of the claim. The deepest IC carries most of this (median 0.30); it is spread over depth in 9 of 18 mice. With the six confined ICs, which leave the spread ICs out, ICs 1-3 average 0.086 ± 0.079 (outside 0.14 ± 0.04) and ICs 4-6 0.061 ± 0.067 (within 0.08 ± 0.03), superficial larger with rank-sum p = 0.0089, so the claim fails under that reading too.
deviations: The gamma ICA (STAR Methods, Independent Component Analysis of LFPs) is fitted on up to 600 s of waking per mouse (the longest `Awake` epochs of at least 30 s), with scikit-learn's FastICA on the first ten PCs of the 30-100 Hz LFP in place of runica (EEGLAB infomax, not available in Python); the whole-session reading of fig2c is not run.
ICs are numbered by the depth of their peak loading; the six are the highest-variance ones (fig2c reading a).
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: Slow oscillation power (0.5-3 Hz) is dominant in non-REM sleep and largest in the deeper layers.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 1; Figures 3C, S3D
outcomes.quote: Slow oscillation power (0.5–3 Hz) was dominant in non-REM sleep ... especially in deeper layers
outcomes.notes: The state part holds: 0.5-3 Hz power (mean over sites) is highest in non-REM (median over mice 6,594 against 5,268 in waking and 1,514 in REM uV^2/Hz; Kruskal-Wallis p = 5.3e-5). Power differs across the six layers in non-REM (p = 9.8e-6 with coherence layers, 2.5e-6 with IC layers), but the largest is in the fourth layer under both readings (normalized medians 1.47 and 1.44; fifth 1.42 and 1.43; sixth 0.95 and 0.80), not in the deepest two.
deviations: Power is the Welch spectrum (4096-sample segments) of up to 600 s of each state, averaged over the band, a standard choice equal in its band mean to a wavelet power average.
Coherence layers are the waking six-cluster solution of fig2b (reading b); IC layers assign each site to the nearest peak of the six main ICs.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: In non-REM sleep the slow oscillation phase modulates gamma amplitude in superficial layers (69 ± 12 Hz, modulation index 2.7 ± 0.5 × 10^-3) and high gamma (>100 Hz) in deep layers (modulation index 2.3 ± 0.3 × 10^-3).
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 1; Figure 3D, left
outcomes.quote: Slow oscillation was phase-coupled to gamma frequency power in superficial layers (69 ± 12 Hz; modulation index 2.7 ± 0.5 × 10 −3 ) and to the high-gamma (>100 Hz) band in deep layers
outcomes.notes: With the 1-3 Hz phase of the layer 6 site in non-REM (reading a), the index averaged over the sites above the layer 4 site peaks at 70.9 ± 16.2 Hz over 18 mice (69 ± 12), within tolerance. The indices are larger than the paper's: 0.0053 ± 0.0039 superficially (0.0027 ± 0.0005) and 0.0028 ± 0.0019 deep (0.0023 ± 0.0003). With the rule's b (16 mice) the values are 70.6 Hz, 0.0051 and 0.0026; with the 0.5-3 Hz phase (reading b), 70.7 Hz, 0.0078 and 0.0048. The superficial coupling at about 70 Hz holds; the index values do not. The deep part of the statement does not hold as stated either: below c the index peaks above 100 Hz in only 5 of 18 mice (6 with the 0.5-3 Hz phase), and its peak over 5-200 Hz has a median of 71 Hz; the criterion's deep index, the largest above 100 Hz, falls at a median of 185 Hz (range 105-200).
deviations: Tort et al. (2008) modulation index with 18 phase bins; the phase band is band-passed (3rd-order Butterworth, zero phase) and its phase taken by the Hilbert transform; amplitudes are Morlet (w0 = 6) amplitudes at 24 log-spaced frequencies from 5 to 200 Hz on every other site; up to 600 s of the state per mouse; the index is averaged over the sites of each region before the peak is taken. The surrogate test of the STAR Methods is not run, as no criterion uses it.

The layer 6 phase site is 15 sites (300 um) below c, the MUA peak of mid layer 5, an assumption: landmark d cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives, and the coherence boundary that opens the sixth layer lies a median 12.5 sites below c (fig2b). In YMV09, where c is at site 56, the site is clipped to the deepest site (7 below c).

Sites above landmark b are read as the sites above the layer 4 site of the ICs; the rule's b is a variant. The layer 4 site is the peak loading site of the third of the six highest-variance gamma ICs ordered by depth, an assumption: landmark b cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives, and Figures S3B and S3D label the six LFP layers L2, L3, L4, L5a, L5b, L6, so the third is layer 4.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: Slow gamma (30-60 Hz) dominates in superficial layers, most in waking, then REM, then non-REM sleep.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 1; Figures 3, S3B, S3D
outcomes.quote: Slow gamma oscillations (30–60 Hz) dominated in superficial layers, especially in the waking state followed by REM and non-REM sleep
outcomes.notes: Over coherence clusters 1-2, 30-60 Hz power is highest in waking, then REM, then non-REM (medians 37.8, 30.7 and 24.2 uV^2/Hz, 18 mice); Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.0025 (reading a); signed-rank waking against REM p = 0.00025 (16 of 18 mice) and REM against non-REM p = 0.00053 (17 of 18) (reading b). The criterion tests only this state order. The statement's "dominates in superficial layers" does not hold here, as in waking, 30-60 Hz power in coherence cluster 1 lies below the mean over sites (median difference -7.06 uV^2/Hz).
deviations: Clusters are the waking six-cluster coherence solution (fig2b reading b); power as in fig3c-slow-oscillation-nrem-deep.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: The most prominent LFP pattern in the waking mouse is a 3-6 Hz oscillation with largest power in layer 4.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figure 3C, level b
outcomes.quote: The most prominent LFP pattern in the waking mouse was a 3–6 Hz oscillation with largest power in layer 4
outcomes.notes: Mean-subtracted waking 3-6 Hz power differs across the six layers (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.022 with coherence layers, 0.0013 with IC layers) and is highest in the third layer under both (medians 289 and 224 uV^2/Hz above the site mean). The layer holding the rule's landmark b ranges from the first to the fifth across mice, so the reading through b is not run.
deviations: Layer 4, defined in the criterion as the layer containing landmark b, is read as the third of the six layers from the surface, as Figures S3B and S3D label them (L2, L3, L4, L5a, L5b, L6); an assumption, as b cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives.
Power as in fig3c-slow-oscillation-nrem-deep, over up to 600 s of waking.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: In waking the 3-6 Hz rhythm is phase-coupled to a 15-25 Hz signal in multiple layers (22 ± 5 Hz, modulation index 4.8 ± 1.2 × 10^-4), to high gamma in superficial layers (90 ± 13 Hz, 2.7 ± 0.7 × 10^-4) and to the epsilon band (>100 Hz) in layer 5 (6.4 ± 1.8 × 10^-4).
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figure 3D, right
outcomes.quote: The 3–6 Hz band was cross-frequency phase-coupled to a 15–25 Hz band signal in multiple layers (22 ± 5 Hz, modulation index 4.8 ± 1.2 × 10 −4 )
outcomes.notes: With the 3-6 Hz phase of the layer 4 site in all waking, over 18 mice: the peak in 10-40 Hz of the index averaged over all sites is at 22.0 ± 5.2 Hz (22 ± 5) with index 1.4 × 10^-4 (4.8 ± 1.2 × 10^-4); the peak in 60-100 Hz above the layer 4 site is at 83.5 ± 11 Hz (90 ± 13) with index 2.6 × 10^-4 (2.7 ± 0.7 × 10^-4); the largest index above 100 Hz over coherence clusters 4-5 (layer 5) is 3.1 × 10^-4 (6.4 ± 1.8 × 10^-4). Three of the five values are within tolerance; the 15-25 Hz and layer 5 indices are lower. The waking-immobility reading cannot be run (the dataset holds no movement signal).
deviations: Tort et al. (2008) modulation index with 18 phase bins; the phase band is band-passed (3rd-order Butterworth, zero phase) and its phase taken by the Hilbert transform; amplitudes are Morlet (w0 = 6) amplitudes at 24 log-spaced frequencies from 5 to 200 Hz on every other site; up to 600 s of the state per mouse; the index is averaged over the sites of each region before the peak is taken. The surrogate test of the STAR Methods is not run, as no criterion uses it.

The layer 4 site is the peak loading site of the third of the six highest-variance gamma ICs ordered by depth, an assumption: landmark b cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives, and Figures S3B and S3D label the six LFP layers L2, L3, L4, L5a, L5b, L6, so the third is layer 4.

The 15-25 Hz coupling "in multiple layers" is read as the peak in 10-40 Hz of the index averaged over all sites; layer 5 as coherence clusters 4 and 5 (L5a, L5b) of the waking six-cluster solution (fig2b).
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: The 3-6 Hz rhythm vanishes with movement; its power is negatively correlated with hippocampal theta power.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 3; Figure S2C
outcomes.quote: The antagonism between movement and the 3–6 Hz oscillation was quantified by the negative correlation between its power and the power of theta oscillation (p < 0.01, signed rank test; Figure S2 C)
outcomes.notes: In waking, 3-6 Hz power at the layer 4 site correlates positively with 6-9 Hz power at the deepest site (median Spearman rho 0.08, negative in 1 of 18 mice with the wavelet time base, 5 of 18 with 10 s windows) and at the same site (0.45 and 0.41, negative in none). The signed-rank tests reject zero in the positive direction at p < 0.01 in three of the four comparisons; with 10 s windows at the deepest site p = 0.01.
deviations: The layer 4 site is the peak loading site of the third of the six highest-variance gamma ICs ordered by depth, an assumption: landmark b cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives, and Figures S3B and S3D label the six LFP layers L2, L3, L4, L5a, L5b, L6, so the third is layer 4.

Theta is read at the deepest site, nearest the hippocampus, as the Results call it volume conducted; the same site is a variant. Wavelet amplitudes (4 frequencies per band) are sampled at 10 Hz; Spearman correlations.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: Both principal cells and interneurons are strongly phase-locked to the trough of the layer 4 3-6 Hz rhythm.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figure 3F
outcomes.quote: Both principal cells and interneurons were strongly phase-locked to the trough of the layer 4-recorded 3–6 Hz rhythm
outcomes.notes: Of 965 E cells with at least 50 waking spikes, 639 are significantly locked to the 3-6 Hz LFP of the layer 4 site, with circular mean preferred phase 187 degrees (trough 180; resultant 0.73, Rayleigh p = 1.2e-175); of 230 I cells, 193 are locked, mean 182 degrees (resultant 0.80, p = 1.3e-66). Mouse means range from 110 to 236 degrees.
deviations: The layer 4 site is the peak loading site of the third of the six highest-variance gamma ICs ordered by depth, an assumption: landmark b cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives, and Figures S3B and S3D label the six LFP layers L2, L3, L4, L5a, L5b, L6, so the third is layer 4.
The phase is that of a Morlet wavelet (w0 = 6) at 4.24 Hz, the geometric centre of 3-6 Hz, with peaks at 0 degrees.
YMV19 has no state table and is left out.

outcomes.statement: Visual stimulation blocks an ongoing 3-6 Hz rhythm, and the offset of a stimulus often induces a short rebound train of 3-6 Hz oscillation.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 3; Figure S2D (cited as S2I)
outcomes.quote: Visual stimulation also blocked an ongoing 3–6 Hz rhythm. However, the offset of visual stimulus often induced a short rebound train 3–6 Hz oscillation
outcomes.notes: Needs the 400 ms flash times across mice; the dataset holds them for 2 of the 13 stimulated mice (YMV05 and YMV08, 498 intervals of 0.4 s each), too few for a test across mice (the smallest two-sided signed-rank p with 2 mice is 0.5). No other file holds visual stimulus times: the groups under acquisition, processing and stimulus of every file are listed in the notebook. The layer 4 site could be taken from the gamma ICs (fig3f-units-lock-3-6hz-trough).

outcomes.statement: The waking 3-6 Hz rhythm has spike and wave waveforms and a depth profile similar to the alpha rhythm in monkey V1.
outcomes.source: Results, Brain State-Dependent Features of LFPs, paragraph 2; Figures 3A, 3B
outcomes.quote: in which the waveforms occasionally split into short “spike” and longer “wave” components with a depth profile distribution similar to the depth distribution of alpha waves (8–12 Hz) in monkey V1
outcomes.notes: The criterion records this claim as methods_underspecified; the paper compares with published monkey figures (Bollimunta et al. 2008) and gives no measure of similarity. Not run.
outcomes.where: Bollimunta et al. 2008, J. Neurosci. 28, 9976-9988, doi:10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2699-08.2008 (published figure, no deposit)

outcomes.statement: Clustering one session from each of the 19 mice yields 1,472 units, with 251 narrow-waveform putative interneurons and 1,075 wide-waveform putative principal cells.
outcomes.source: Results, Assignment of Neurons to Physiologically Defined Layers, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: Unit clustering was performed as described previously ( Fujisawa et al., 2008 ) using one session from each of the 19 mice, yielding a total of 1,472 units
outcomes.notes: 1,477 units in the files (1,476 of quality good; 1,472 ± 147). From the wide-band mean waveform, as the Results describe ("the unfiltered waveform was quantified by the trough-to-peak latency", Assignment of Neurons to Physiologically Defined Layers, paragraph 1), 246 narrow I cells (251 ± 25) and 1,016 wide E cells (1,075 ± 108); 105 positive units, no fiber unit, and 110 units with fewer than 10 spikes in the 60 s used. With a 300 Hz high-pass the counts are 320 and 941, both outside tolerance. At thresholds of 0.50 and 0.60 ms the I count is 215 and 323. Each mouse contributes 5 to 20 I cells.
deviations: The dataset holds no waveforms; mean waveforms are averaged from 60 s of raw signal per session (two 30 s blocks at 1000 and 3000 s, median 127 spikes per unit), where the paper used all spikes, and 110 units with fewer than 10 spikes there are left unclassified.

The wide-band signal follows the Results' unfiltered waveform; the STAR Methods do not say whether the waveform is filtered, and the 300 Hz high-pass of Kilosort is shown as a variant, which does not match.
The fiber rule reads the STAR Methods' kurtosis of the second derivative of the normalized waveform, with units beyond the mean ± 5 SD of the negative units as fibers; none is.

outcomes.statement: Short-latency CCG interactions identify 347 E and 100 I cells, and these agree with the waveform classes (97.4% of CCG-based E cells are waveform E cells; 98.0% of CCG-based I cells are waveform I cells).

findings.statement: The 520 nm flash times behind the visual evoked CSD (Figure 1E, 1F, S2D) are in 2 of the 13 stimulated mice, as the `Visual laser` tables of YMV05 and YMV08 (498 intervals of 0.4 s each). The other files hold no visual stimulus times.

The `Visual laser` tables ("Laser pulses for subject stimulation") of YMV05 and YMV08 also hold the optogenetic pulses of the `Laser diode` table (1,488 and 2,715 of their intervals start within 5 ms of a `Laser diode` pulse), and one YMV05 interval lasts 49.6 s.

The genotypes in the files are 11 PV-Cre::Ai32 and 3 VGAT-Cre::Ai32 mice; the paper's STAR Methods give 5 PV-Cre::Ai32 and 9 VGAT-Cre::Ai32. The other genotypes (3 Ai35, 1 CaMKII-Cre::Ai35, 1 CaMKII-Cre::Ai32) agree.

The electrode table gives no depth or position (x, y and z are NaN, location "unknown", impedance -1); only rel_y (-1 to -64) implies the site order. The data are consistent with the columns being in that depth order (for each file the best-correlated site in the 100-500 Hz LFP is an adjacent one for 50 to 63 of the 64 sites). The units carry no waveform, layer, depth, landmark or cluster label, so every laminar analysis of the paper must be rebuilt from the raw signal and LFP.

The units' `max_channel` holds the electrode table `id` (a hardware channel number; the ids are a permutation of 0 to 63) of the unit's peak site: it equals the id of the column of the unit's largest mean waveform for 1,157 of 1,255 units (1,247 within one site), and the column index for 76. The column description ("Channel that observed the maximum waveform amplitude") does not say which numbering it uses.

The `cell_type` labels (Pyramidal Cell 836, Narrow Interneuron 277, Wide Interneuron 223, Unknown 15, down state 10) follow a scheme the paper does not describe; 198 "Wide Interneuron" units have a waveform E trough-to-peak latency. The 10 "down state" units are in 6 mice, where the paper reports 5 DOWN state-active neurons in 4 mice. The `synaptic_effect` labels (444 Excitatory, 145 Inhibitory) do not match the paper's 347 CCG-based E and 100 I cells, and their rule is not given.
YMV03 has no unit columns but quality (no cell_type, synaptic_effect, max_channel or firing_rate), and one of its units is "unsorted". YMV19 has no Sleep states table.
YMV07, a CaMKII-Cre::Ai35 mouse, has 41,022 laser pulses of 20 ms at one level, a protocol the paper does not describe.

Question for the paper's authors. How were the CSD landmarks a, b, d and e chosen on the DOWN-UP CSD map? The paper calls them "the most prominent" sinks and sources and marks them by hand in Figure 1D. A rule that takes the extreme CSD above and below the MUA peak places them inconsistently (adjacent distances ranging by 220 to 620 um across mice), so normalized depth and every layer group of the paper cannot be rebuilt from the text.

Question for the paper's authors. Which LFP site gives the phases of the spike-LFP coupling of Figure S7 (the unit's own site, a fixed layer, or an IC)? With the unit's own site the unit's spike dominates the high frequencies; 10 sites away 3-6 Hz is strongest but 0.5-3 Hz is second and 30-60 Hz fifth.

Question for the paper's authors. Were further selections applied in the monosynaptic detection (for example on pairs recorded on the same or neighbouring sites, on firing rates, or by refractory contamination)? The rule of the STAR Methods applied to these units finds 1,295 excitatory and 578 inhibitory connections and 673 and 187 CCG-based E and I cells, about twice the paper's 525, 323, 347 and 100, and the pair count of 102,332 matches no count of pairs of the 1,477 units.

Question for the paper's authors. How were the eight unit clusters obtained: on the spike-IC coupling matrix or on its t-SNE embedding, with which features per unit (the full 6 IC x 20 scale profile or one value per IC), and over which range of cluster numbers was the silhouette compared? Under each of these readings the silhouette here favours 2 to 6 clusters, never 8, and the eight-cluster solutions do not separate depth as Figure 5C does.

Question for the paper's authors. Which components count as volume conducted in the 0.34 ± 0.11 of gamma variance, and how were the six main ICs chosen among the ten? Here the ten PCs hold 0.99 of the band variance, the six of highest variance include a deep component that carries up to 0.71 of it, and the spread components carry 0.53.

entries.title: Layer-specific features of mouse V1 units (Senzai et al. 2019)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Senzai, Fernandez-Ruiz and Buzsaki (2019) on dandiset 000166, which holds one session from each of 19 mice recorded with a 64-site linear probe in V1, with spike-sorted units, LFP, the raw signal, brain state and UP/DOWN intervals and laser pulse times. It tests the unit counts and waveform classes, the CCG-based detection of monosynaptic connections, the optogenetic tagging, the gamma ICA and coherence clusters, the laminar LFP power, cross-frequency coupling and 3-6 Hz phase locking, the K-means unit clusters and the layer features of firing and connections that rest on them, and the DOWN state-active neurons. Depth is aligned on the MUA power peak, as the CSD landmarks cannot be placed by a rule the paper gives.
